title: The 'Missing Men' of the American Marriage Market: How Education Gaps Are Reshaping Who Gets Hitched
summary: What if the dating world worked like a market, with supply and demand shaping who ends up with whom? That's the lens economists use, and a new study suggests it explains a lot about why marriage in America is changing—and not equally for everyone. First, a quirky story: musician Jack Antonoff once joked that he dated Scarlett Johansson in high school because he transferred to an arts school where he was 'the only straight kid in the class.' The gender imbalance worked in his favor. It's a lighthearted example of a serious phenomenon: when one group is scarce, their 'value' in the dating market can rise. Now zoom out to the U.S. marriage market. For decades, women have been outpacing men in education. Female students now make up nearly 60% of undergraduates, outnumbering men by over two million. At the same time, many men without college degrees face economic headwinds—stagnant wages, higher unemployment, and greater risks of incarceration or substance abuse. Enter the working paper 'Bachelors Without Bachelor's: Gender Gaps in Education and Declining Marriage Rates' by economists Clara Chambers, Benjamin Goldman, and Joseph Winkelmann. Their findings are striking: college-educated women have largely maintained high marriage rates, but they're increasingly 'marrying down' educationally—pairing with men who didn't finish college. Crucially, they're not settling for just any man; they're selecting the highest earners from that pool. This creates a ripple effect. Women without a college degree are left with a depleted supply of economically stable men. Their marriage rates have plummeted, even as they continue to have children, leading to a surge in single-mother households. The researchers call this a 'missing men' phenomenon—not missing in numbers, but missing in economic stability. It's a stark parallel to post-WWI France, where a shortage of men let survivors 'marry up,' or modern China, where a surplus of men (thanks to the one-child policy) gave women more leverage. In America, the imbalance isn't about raw numbers but about diverging fortunes. The consequences are profound: widening inequality, less family stability, and a redefinition of who gets to participate in the institution of marriage. As The Beatles sang, money can't buy love—but it sure seems to influence who gets a chair when the music stops.
why_it_matters: This story reveals how shifts in education and the economy ripple into personal life, shaping who gets married and which families stay stable. For a teenager, it’s a preview of a world where your future relationships may be influenced not just by love, but by earnings, degrees, and broader economic trends.

background_read: The study's authors—Clara Chambers, Benjamin Goldman, and Joseph Winkelmann (economics researchers who focus on families and inequality)—were not the first to notice that American marriage patterns are changing. For decades, sociologists have tracked the education gap: women began earning more bachelor's degrees than men in the early 1980s, and the gap has only widened.

Economically, many jobs that once paid a middle-class wage to men without college degrees (manufacturing, construction) have declined. Meanwhile, incarceration rates in the U.S. rose sharply from the 1970s through the 2000s, disproportionately affecting men with less education. Substance abuse and 'deaths of despair' have also hit working-class men hard, shrinking the pool of stable partners.

Historical parallels help explain the 'scarcity' idea: after World War I, France lost so many young men that survivors could marry above their pre-war social class. In China, the one-child policy (1979–2015) led to a surplus of men, giving women more leverage in the marriage market. The U.S. case is different—it's not about raw numbers but economic viability.

└─ specific: He joked he was 'the only straight kid in the class,' giving him an edge in dating.
MAIN ARGUMENT: Economists treat the dating world like a market where supply and demand shape who pairs with whom.
├─ CONTEXT: For decades, women have outpaced men in education; nearly 60% of undergraduates are female, men face economic headwinds.
└─ STUDY FINDINGS: The working paper 'Bachelors Without Bachelor's' reveals college-educated women are 'marrying down' educationally but selecting the highest-earning men without degrees.
RIPPLE EFFECT: Women without college degrees are left with fewer economically stable men; their marriage rates have plummeted, leading to more single-mother households.
HISTORICAL PARALLELS: Similar dynamics in post-WWI France (survivors 'married up') and modern China (surplus of men gave women leverage).
CONSEQUENCES: Widening inequality, less family stability, and a redefinition of who can participate in the institution of marriage—summed up with a Beatles lyric.

perspectives.description: College-educated women are still marrying at high rates and can choose economically stable partners even if those men lack degrees. The most capable men without college degrees—high earners—gain access to the marriage market in ways they might not have before.

Women without college degrees face a severely depleted pool of reliable partners, leading to plunging marriage rates and a rise in single-mother households. This widens inequality and can trap families in cycles of poverty, as children grow up with less financial stability.

The 'marriage market' lens shows that shifts in education and employment are not just personal troubles but systemic patterns—similar to how labor markets work. The U.S. is not the first society to experience such an imbalance; post-war France and China’s gender-ratio distortions offer real-world comparisons.

Policies that improve job prospects and wages for men without college degrees—or that make higher education more accessible for all—could help rebalance the marriage market. Alternatively, if current trends continue, we may see a permanent split in family formation, where marriage becomes largely a practice of the well-educated.
